approved: Corporations Legislation Amendment (Deregulatory and Other Measures) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would cut red tape for businesses and the community by changing company law.
It would change rules on shareholder meetings, pay reporting, financial years, auditors, takeover procedures and the Remuneration Tribunal's role.
The explanatory memorandum does not give a start date.
Balance shareholder rights against the cost of calling general meetings.
Reduce reporting requirements on executive pay.
Clarify when a financial year may be shorter than 12 months.
Let some companies limited by guarantee skip appointing or keeping an auditor.
Allow the Takeovers Panel to handle matters more efficiently.
Give the Remuneration Tribunal power to set pay for certain bodies under the Corporations Act.
Businesses and the community subject to the Corporations Act 2001 and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act 2001.

Explained Labor's support for the Corporations Legislation Amendment (Deregulatory and Other Measures) Bill, including repeal of the 100-member rule that let shareholders force costly general meetings, noting a $500,000 meeting called over poker machine limits that won just 2.5 per cent support, and backed reduced remuneration reporting and auditor requirements for smaller entities.

Supported the deregulation bill, cited the government's two 2014 repeal days that removed more than 10,000 pieces of legislation and cut $2.1 billion in compliance costs, and referenced a Productivity Commission estimate that regulation compliance could cost up to four per cent of Australia's GDP.

Supported the Corporations Legislation Amendment (Deregulatory and Other Measures) Bill, explaining that it lets a general meeting still be forced by five per cent of shareholders instead of 100, removes the requirement to report lapsed share options, and allows Takeovers Panel members to perform their duties from overseas.

Supported the Corporations Legislation Amendment (Deregulatory and Other Measures) Bill, citing about $14 million a year in compliance savings, and highlighted a Woolworths shareholder meeting forced by 210 of 417,000 shareholders that cost the company nearly $2 million.

Challenged Labor's claim to have long supported repealing the 100-member rule, tracing reform attempts back to 2000, detailed the 2012 Woolworths case where GetUp forced a meeting costing nearly $2 million despite winning almost no shareholder support, and noted a 2005 Labor minority report that proposed capping the threshold at 1500 members instead of abolishing it.

Supported the Corporations Legislation Amendment (Deregulatory and Other Measures) Bill, noting it would raise the threshold to force a general meeting from 100 shareholders to five per cent of votes, saving an estimated $1.5 million a year, and remove remuneration reporting for unlisted entities, saving a further $8.5 million.

Attacked GetUp! over a 2012 stunt in which 204 of its members forced a $2 million meeting of Woolworths shareholders and directors that won just three per cent support, and supported the Corporations Legislation Amendment (Deregulatory and Other Measures) Bill for removing $14 million in compliance costs from Australian businesses.

Supported the Corporations Legislation Amendment (Deregulatory and Other Measures) Bill 2014, recalling from his time as Attorney-General that Australia once had around 80 different pieces of personal property securities legislation across the states and territories, citing a Mount Gambier and Geelong hotel business that needed separate legal advice because floating charges over stock differed between South Australian and Victorian law.

Supported the Corporations Legislation Amendment Bill on behalf of Labor, noting Australia is unusual in allowing 100 shareholders to force a general meeting regardless of their capital held, when most jurisdictions require five to 10 per cent of shares, and recalled the NRMA was forced to call 12 extraordinary general meetings between late 1999 and late 2001 to consider removing directors, at a cost of several million dollars, without any resolution passing.

Supported the Corporations Legislation Amendment Bill, detailing how the 100-member rule forced Woolworths to spend $500,000 notifying shareholders of a meeting on poker machine bet limits that received only 2.5 per cent support, and began citing a further example involving the NRMA raised by shadow minister Bernie Ripoll before being cut off.
